text: This lab is where you stop reading verified numbers and start producing them yourself. You'll run the exact Grover circuit from Lesson 26 and confirm its predicted result, then hand-evaluate the toy VQE cost function from Lesson 28 at points of your own choosing.

Run the exact circuit from Lesson 26 at 1000 shots. The verified prediction is exact and deterministic: all 1000 shots should come back as 11, with no other outcome appearing at all. If your counts dictionary shows anything else, double-check the oracle and the five-gate diffuser block against Lesson 26 before assuming the underlying math is wrong — this is the N=4, M=1 special case with no statistical spread to account for.

Lesson 28 gave you the closed form for the toy Hamiltonian: 0.5 cosine theta plus 0.3 sine theta, plus a table of verified values and the true minimum of negative 0.583095. Now pick three or four theta values of your own, not already in that table, and compute the expectation value by hand — compute cosine and sine, plug into the formula, and compare your result to the known minimum.

This is the real point of the exercise. A gradient-free optimizer like COBYLA, running inside a real VQE loop, never sees the formula — it only sees the numeric result of evaluating the expectation value at whatever theta it chooses to try, exactly like what you just did by hand. Order your computed points by theta, and without using the formula, ask which direction you'd try next to get below negative 0.5. Does your reasoning lead you toward the known true minimum?

It's worth being explicit about why this lab avoids computing a derivative. On real hardware, every expectation-value measurement already costs real quantum shots and queue time — estimating a derivative numerically would mean paying for additional nearby measurements for every optimizer step, on top of whatever noise already sits in each one. Point-evaluation-only optimizers like COBYLA exist specifically because that trade-off is usually worth it.
Chapter 7 goes beyond the simple depolarizing error you've seen so far, into realistic, calibrated noise models, and the real mitigation techniques used to clean up their effects.
